content: The following WHO staff members from the Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infections Programmes contributed to the development and updating of these guidelines: Morkor Newman, Martina Penazzato, Marco Vitoria, and Lara Vojnov. Contributions were also made by regional WHO offices, including Frank Lule (WHO Regional Office for Africa), Omar Sued (Pan American Health Organization), BB Rewari and Mukta Sharma (WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia), Elena Vovc (WHO Regional Office for Europe), and Chan Po-Lin (WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific). The development of these guidelines was supported by a grant from Unitaid to WHO. Cryptococcal disease is one of the most common opportunistic infections among individuals with advanced HIV disease and is a significant cause of illness, disability, and mortality. Cryptococcal meningitis is the most frequent clinical presentation, with an estimated 223,100 incident cases and 181,100 deaths among people living with HIV in 2014, accounting for 15% of all HIV-related deaths globally. Cryptococcal disease is rare in children with HIV. A public health approach focusing on prevention, early diagnosis, and improved treatment of cryptococcal disease and its complications is essential to reduce the incidence and high mortality associated with cryptococcal meningitis, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. These guidelines summarize recommendations first released in 2018 for diagnosing, preventing, and managing cryptococcal disease. In response to new evidence available in 2021, a new recommendation is provided regarding the preferred antifungal regimen for the induction phase of treatment. These updated guidelines replace the 2018 version and were developed following procedures established by the WHO Guideline Review Committee. All recommendations are based on the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, incorporating evidence on acceptability, values, preferences, cost-effectiveness, and feasibility. The guideline development process also identified key knowledge gaps to guide future research. The objective of these guidelines is to provide updated, evidence-informed recommendations for treating adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV who have cryptococcal disease. These guidelines are intended for HIV program managers, policymakers, healthcare professionals, and people living with HIV. Diagnosis of Cryptococcal Meningitis (2018 Recommendations) 1. For adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV suspected of having a first episode of cryptococcal meningitis, a lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure measurement and rapid cryptococcal antigen assay is recommended as the preferred diagnostic approach. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for adults and adolescents and low-certainty evidence for children. 2. In settings where lumbar puncture is accessible and not contraindicated, CSF India ink test examination is recommended if a cryptococcal antigen assay is unavailable or rapid results are not feasible. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for adults and adolescents and low-certainty evidence for children. 3. For a first episode, CSF cryptococcal culture is also recommended alongside cryptococcal antigen testing if feasible. In settings without immediate access to lumbar puncture or when lumbar puncture is clinically contraindicated: 1. If rapid results from a cryptococcal antigen assay (serum, plasma, or whole blood) are available within 24 hours, this is the preferred diagnostic approach. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for adults and adolescents and low-certainty evidence for children. 2. If a cryptococcal antigen assay is unavailable or rapid access to results is not ensured, prompt referral for further investigation and treatment is appropriate. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for adults and adolescents and low-certainty evidence for children. Other diseases presenting with similar symptoms to cryptococcal meningitis (e.g., viral, bacterial, or tuberculous meningitis) should also be considered. Contraindications to lumbar puncture include significant coagulopathy, suspected space-occupying lesions based on focal nervous system signs (excluding cranial nerve VI palsy), recurrent seizures, or confirmed by computed tomography. Raised intracranial pressure does not contraindicate lumbar puncture in suspected cryptococcal meningitis. Other contraindications include major spinal deformity and patient refusal after fully informed consent. Prevention and Screening (2018 Recommendations) Screening for plasma, serum, or whole-blood cryptococcal antigen is the optimal approach for guiding resources in a public health context and is preferred for identifying infection in individuals aged 10 years and older presenting with advanced HIV disease. 1. Screening for cryptococcal antigen followed by pre-emptive antifungal therapy among cryptococcal antigen-positive individuals is recommended to prevent invasive cryptococcal disease before initiating or reinitiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) in adults and adolescents with HIV and a CD4 cell count <100 cells/mm³. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 2. This approach may be considered at a higher CD4 cell count threshold of <200 cells/mm³. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 3. All individuals with a positive cryptococcal antigen screening result should be carefully evaluated for signs and symptoms of meningitis and undergo lumbar puncture, if feasible, with CSF examination and India ink or CSF cryptococcal antigen assay to exclude meningitis. India ink has low sensitivity, and a negative result should be confirmed by CSF cryptococcal antigen testing or CSF culture. If cryptococcal antigen screening is unavailable, fluconazole primary prophylaxis should be given to adults and adolescents with HIV and a CD4 cell count <100 cells/mm³. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. This approach may also be considered at a higher CD4 cell count threshold of <200 cells/mm³. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. Treating Cryptococcal Meningitis (2022 Recommendations) Induction Therapy: A single high dose (10 mg/kg) of liposomal amphotericin B with 14 days of flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day divided into four doses) and fluconazole (1200 mg daily for adults; 12 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents up to a maximum of 800 mg daily) is the preferred induction regimen. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for adults and low-certainty evidence for children. Alternative Induction Regimens: 1. If liposomal amphotericin is unavailable: A seven-day course of amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg/day) and flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day divided into four doses) followed by seven days of fluconazole (1200 mg daily for adults; 12 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents up to a maximum of 800 mg daily). This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for adults and low-certainty evidence for children and adolescents. 2. If no amphotericin formulation is available: 14 days of fluconazole (1200 mg daily for adults; 12 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents) and flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day divided into four doses). This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 3. If flucytosine is unavailable: 14 days of liposomal amphotericin B (3–4 mg/kg/day) and fluconazole (1200 mg daily for adults; 12 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents up to a maximum of 800 mg daily). This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 4. If liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine are unavailable: 14 days of amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg/day) and fluconazole (1200 mg daily for adults; 12 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents up to a maximum of 800 mg daily). This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. Flucytosine-containing regimens are superior, and steps should be taken to ensure access to this drug. Consolidation Phase (2018 Recommendations): Fluconazole (800 mg daily for adults or 6–12 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents up to a maximum of 800 mg daily) is recommended for eight weeks following the induction phase. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. Maintenance Phase (2018 Recommendations): Fluconazole (200 mg daily for adults or 6 mg/kg/day for adolescents and children) is recommended until immune reconstitution (CD4 >200 mm³) and viral load suppression on ART. This is a strong recommendation with high-certainty evidence. Adjunctive Corticosteroids (2018 Recommendations): Routine use of adjunctive corticosteroid therapy during the induction phase is not recommended for treating HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis. This is a strong recommendation with high-certainty evidence for adults and adolescents and moderate-certainty evidence for children. Timing of ART (2018 Recommendations): Immediate ART initiation is not recommended for individuals with cryptococcal meningitis due to the risk of increased mortality. ART should be deferred for 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal treatment. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence for adults and very-low-certainty evidence for children and adolescents. Good Practice Principles Preventing, Monitoring, and Managing Amphotericin B Toxicity (2022): Safe administration of amphotericin B should be prioritized, potentially requiring referral to centers with access to the recommended package for preventing, monitoring, and managing toxicity. Liposomal amphotericin B has fewer risks of drug toxicity than amphotericin B deoxycholate and requires less intensive monitoring. The recommended package for managing toxicity should be provided to minimize serious amphotericin B-related toxicities, especially hypokalaemia, nephrotoxicity, and anaemia. Monitoring Raised Intracranial Pressure (2018): Individuals with suspected cryptococcal meningitis should undergo an initial lumbar puncture and early repeat lumbar puncture with CSF opening pressure measurement to assess for raised intracranial pressure, regardless of symptoms. Repeat therapeutic lumbar punctures are recommended for persistent symptoms until resolution or normalization of opening pressure for at least two days. Monitoring Treatment Response (2018): Clinical response should be assessed daily during the initial two weeks of induction therapy. Routine follow-up lumbar puncture after completing induction therapy to assess antifungal treatment response is not advised in lowand middle-income countries. CSF, serum, or plasma cryptococcal antigen testing is not recommended for monitoring treatment response. Diagnostic Approach to Persistent or Recurrent Symptoms (2018): Review patient history for evidence of treatment failure due to inadequate drug regimen, poor adherence, or underlying fluconazole resistance. Consider paradoxical cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after excluding other causes of recurrent symptoms in individuals who have started ART. Send or resend CSF for prolonged fungal culture (two weeks of incubation).
